disgruntled

/dis-GRUN-tuld/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Disgruntled means annoyed and dissatisfied, usually about a specific complaint or grievance.

The disgruntled diner sent back her cold pasta and asked, for the second time, to speak with the manager.

Example

Marcus had covered every weekend shift for a year, so when the promotion went to a newer hire, he became visibly disgruntled. He muttered about the decision at his desk and started keeping a list of everything he had ever done for the company.

Marcus is not heartbroken or enraged; he is irritated and dissatisfied over one specific grievance, being passed over, which is exactly the grumbling, testy mood disgruntled describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

annoyed: Annoyed is the all-purpose word for mild irritation at anything - a noise, a delay, a person. Disgruntled is more specific: sulkily dissatisfied over a particular grievance, usually a decision or arrangement that went against you. You can be annoyed for a second; disgruntled implies a grudge that lingers and grumbles.

discontented: Discontented describes a settled unhappiness with your overall circumstances - the job, the pay, the way things are. Disgruntled points at one concrete grievance and adds a grumbling, testy edge. A discontented worker wants a different life; a disgruntled one keeps stewing over the promotion that went to someone else.

grumpy: Grumpy is a mood word: bad-tempered and complaining, often for no reason beyond a poor night's sleep. Disgruntled always has a reason - a specific grievance the person could name if asked. A grumpy neighbor snaps at everyone; a disgruntled neighbor is sore about the fence you built.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

pleased: happy with how things are

satisfied: content because expectations were met

Where it sits · how deep and hot the anger runs — miffed → disgruntled → furious

miffed vs. disgruntled: Miffed describes a small, passing flash of annoyance, while disgruntled suggests a deeper, grumbling dissatisfaction over a specific grievance.

furious vs. disgruntled: Disgruntled stops well short of furious, which describes open, intense anger rather than testy dissatisfaction.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — dis-

Prefix — dis-: thoroughly (an intensifier here, not negation)

Root — gruntle

Root — gruntle: to grumble (an archaic English word)

Suffix — -ed

Suffix — -ed: having that quality (adjective-forming)

Put it together

Put it together: Here dis- works as an intensifier meaning 'thoroughly,' not as 'not': gruntle is an old English word meaning 'to grumble,' so disgruntled literally means 'grumbling thoroughly.' There is no everyday positive word 'gruntled'; the prefixed form simply outlived its base word.

Use the root in a new word: grunt

Use the root in a new word: grunt: The old dog gave a low grunt of protest when the kids tried to move it off the couch.

Word Choice

Everyday, mildly informal

Disgruntled almost always points to one concrete grievance: a fee, a delay, a decision that went against someone. Unlike disaffected (loss of loyalty to an authority or institution) or disheartened (loss of hope or morale), disgruntled centers on irritation over one specific grievance, usually with a grumbling, testy tone.
